title: These are the words
hook: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell speech, retelling forty years
tomorrow: Devarim: the man of few words speaks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book of Numbers ended on the plains of Moab, a new generation at the river, and we said chazak. Your line was at the edge. What's about to begin for you? Today, a new book. Day four hundred eighty-one.

Near the end of a life, some people want to tell their story. Not the whole thing, start to finish, but the parts that mattered, told their way, to the people who'll go on without them. Grandparents do it at the kitchen table. Teachers do it in a last lecture. The fifth book of the Torah is that kind of telling. Tradition says Moses has only weeks left. The people are camped across from the land he will never enter. And he begins to talk.
screen: `THE PARTS THAT MATTERED.` → `A FEW WEEKS LEFT.` → `AND HE BEGINS TO TALK.`

segments.voice: The book opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan." In Hebrew, Eleh ha-devarim. These are the words. And that gives the book its Hebrew name: Devarim, words. The English name, Deuteronomy, comes from the old Greek translation and means something like second law, from a phrase inside the book about a copy of the teaching. The rabbis sometimes called it Mishneh Torah, the repetition of the Torah. Both names catch something. Much of what Moses says, we've heard before: the Ten Commandments, the spies, the golden calf, laws about festivals and justice. But this time it's not the narrator telling it. It's Moses, mostly speaking in his own voice, to a generation that was too young to remember, or wasn't born yet. And memory isn't a recording. When Moses retells the spies, for example, he says it was the people who first asked to send them, a detail that isn't in the version we read in Numbers. This is the story as he lived it, and wants them to keep it. The book opens on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year. By the end of it, Moses has died. Jewish tradition counts the time between as only a few weeks. So the whole book is a farewell: one long last conversation. A new part of the path begins here, portion by portion through Moses' last words. Before anything else, notice the frame. The final thing the Torah gives us is a person speaking to the people he loves.
screen: `ELEH HA-DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.` · `DEUTERONOMY: A SECOND TELLING.` · `THE STORY AS MOSES LIVED IT.` · `ONE LONG LAST CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a short farewell to something. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're leaving behind, or already have: a home, a job, a season of life, a habit, someone who has died, even a younger version of yourself. If you have paper, write three or four lines to it. What did it give you? What do you want to remember? What would you say if you could? If you don't have paper, compose the lines in your mind. Let them be simple and true. Breathe with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, the book of Moses' farewell, from its opening line: these are the words.
Your line: last words matter. Today, when you say goodbye to someone, even for an afternoon, make the last thing you say a kind one. Day four hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Deuteronomy is read in synagogue from midsummer to early fall, ending on Simchat Torah, and its first portion, Devarim, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, or on the day itself when Tisha B'Av falls on the Sabbath and the fast is postponed.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you have a few weeks left, and the people at the river were children or unborn when it all began. what do you do?
options: write them a new code of law and leave.
tell them the whole story again, in your own words.
spend your last weeks alone on the mountain.
fork.reveal: he tells it again: the journey, the laws, the mistakes, as he lived them. that's the book of Devarim.

original.note: Hebrew: words, things; the Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, from its first verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fifth book that repeats the first four.
what it means: Moses' farewell, the story retold in his own voice to a new generation.

what a scholar hears: 'Deuteronomy' comes via the Greek of 17:18's mishneh ha-torah, 'a copy of this law'; the book opens on 1 Shevat of the fortieth year (1:3), and tradition dates Moses' death to 7 Adar.

sources.quoted: These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan.

notes: Deuteronomy 1:1 JPS 1917: confirm 'These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan'.
Deuteronomy 1:3: first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year; tradition (Seder Olam) has Moses speak Deuteronomy over his last 36–37 days, dying 7 Adar. The script says 'a few weeks'.
Deuteronomy 1:22 (people ask to send scouts) vs Numbers 13:1–2 (God tells Moses to send them); Rashi harmonizes. Confirm framing.
Block D (Deuteronomy) opens here; Exodus 4:10 ('not a man of words') is left for tomorrow's lesson.
